claims.text: Range: the sources ask for a full range, heels as low as they comfortably go and as high as possible. How deep differs: one says a full stretch below the platform, one as much as comfortably possible, and one warns not to overstretch; the card follows a full but comfortable stretch.

quotes.text: Lower heels until calves are fully stretched below platform; raise until ankles are fully extended with heels highest possible.
Focus on a full range of motion, lowering your heels as much as possible and raising them as high as you can.
Lower your heels towards the ground, stretching your calf muscles as much as comfortably possible. This is your starting position.

quotes.text: Do not overstretch your calves during the negative portion of the exercise.

claims.text: Stay upright with the back straight and the core engaged, looking straight ahead, not down at the feet.

Keep your back straight and your core engaged. Look straight ahead and not down at your feet.

claims.text: Breathe out as the heels rise and in as they lower.

claims.text: The calves are the target: the standing calf raise trains both calf muscles, the soleus and the gastrocnemius, at once. In the seated version the soleus is emphasized and the gastrocnemius takes a secondary role; standing, all three calf muscles share top billing.

quotes.text: Calves
Standing calf raises train both the inner (solues) and outer (gastrocnemius) calf muscles simultaneously.
So, while seated calf raises emphasize the soleus muscle and the gastrocnemius and plantaris take a secondary role, during standing calf raises, all three muscles share top billing.
quotes.where: Standing Calf Raise: The Basics, Muscles Worked

claims.text: In 14 untrained adults training one leg standing (knee straight) and the other seated (knee bent 90 degrees) for 12 weeks, the gastrocnemius grew much more on the standing leg (lateral 12.4% vs 1.7%, medial 9.2% vs 0.6%) and the soleus grew about the same; the authors recommend the standing calf raise for gastrocnemius growth.

quotes.text: Fourteen untrained adults conducted calf-raise training with one leg in a standing/knee-extended position and the other leg in a seated/knee 90°-flexed position at 70% of one-repetition maximum.
Each leg performed 10 repetitions/set, 5 sets/session, 2 sessions/week for 12 weeks.

The changes in muscle volume were significantly greater for the standing than seated condition leg in the lateral gastrocnemius (12.4% vs. 1.7%), medial gastrocnemius (9.2% vs. 0.6%), and whole triceps surae (5.6% vs. 2.1%) (p ≤ 0.011), but similar between legs in the soleus (2.1% vs. 2.9%, p = 0.410).
Standing calf-raise was by far more effective, therefore recommended, than seated calf-raise for inducing muscle hypertrophy of the gastrocnemius and consequently the whole triceps surae.

quotes.text: Stop if sharp pain occurs

claims.text: With the load on the shoulders, heavy standing calf raises put a lot of vertical stress on the spine, which can compress the discs and could even cause back pain; with lower back issues, go cautiously.

quotes.text: With the load resting on your shoulders, heavy calf raises put a lot of vertical stress on your spine, which can cause compression of the intervertebral disks. In short, this exercise could make you temporarily shorter and could even cause back pain.
quotes.where: Standing Calf Raise – Cons, Spinal Compression and Lower Back Stress

quotes.text: However, if you have any lower back issues, you may want to proceed cautiously with standing calf raises, as they may exacerbate it.
quotes.where: Standing Calf Raise – Cons, Spinal Compression and Lower Back Stress

quotes.text: Choose a weight that allows you to perform 10-12 reps with good form. If you’re new to this exercise, start lighter and work your way up.

plate.viewWhy: Census view is side; the knee bend (the top fault, locked knees, c5, c6), the heels dropping below and rising above the platform edge (c9, c7) and the upright trunk under the pads (c2, c11) read from the side.
plate.equipment: Standing calf raise machine (census calfMachine, compose): shoulder pads set to the lifter's height (c1), a raised platform edge under the balls of the feet with the heels free (c1), handles by the pads (c2, c3).
plate.start: Bottom of the rep: standing upright with the shoulders under the pads (c2, c11); balls of the feet on the platform edge, feet parallel and hip-width apart (c1, c4); knees slightly bent (c5); heels lowered below the platform to a full but comfortable stretch (c9, c10); hands on the handles (c2, c3). No source gives joint angles.
plate.end: Top of the rep: heels raised as high as possible, ankles fully extended (c7, c10); knees still slightly bent, trunk upright, unchanged from the start (c5, c11).

mistake.what: Knees locked straight while the heels rise and lower.
mistake.why: Locking the knees is on Motra's common-mistakes list (c6); Motra says to keep a slight knee bend to protect the joints, and Fitness Volt to keep the knees slightly bent but stable to avoid strain (c5).
mistake.rankNote: No source measures how often each fault happens. LR-31 step 2: locking the knees (c6, c5). Candidates: the load is not a candidate, so Motra's list item "Using too much weight" (c6) and "Avoid excessive weight to prevent Achilles strain" (c15) are set aside; setting the shoulder pads (c1) is a setup choice. Step 1: no frequency word for a fault of this exercise. Set aside: Fitness Volt's "the standing calf raise is arguably the most common and popular choice", "Most gyms have a standing calf raise machine" and "when most people talk about calf raises, it’s standing calf raises that they’re referring to" are about the exercise, its machines and its name; its "some lifters find building bigger calves easy" is about training; its seated lines ("The seated calf raise is often overshadowed by the standing variation", "usually tucked away in the corner of the gym", "Most seated calf machines require very few adjustments", "they’re often awkward or inconvenient compared to using a machine") are another exercise; "The standing calf raise machine is popular, common, and easy to use." is about the machine; "The most critical calf training decision that most people have to make is choosing between seated and standing calf raises." is an exercise choice; "training them often involves heavy loads" is about the load; its summary rows "Easier to master; less likely to result in form errors." (seated) and "May require more attention to form, especially for beginners." name no fault; "That’s because the calves tend to work hardest when standing" uses 'tend' and is about muscles; "overweight people often have large calves", "women, who often don’t want big calves", "For most people, this means 2-3 calf workouts per week", "This is usually easiest if you spread those sets over several workouts.", "some people believe the gastrocnemius responds best to lower reps" and "remember your calves won’t grow if you don’t train them hard and often" are about people, programming and training. Motra's "Popularity Score" ("How commonly this exercise is used in training programs") is about the exercise. Pages read but not cited: BarBend's best-calf-exercises ("most people have a stubborn muscle group", about training) and ACE's barbell and straight-leg machine calf raise pages (no frequency word); Peloton's calf-raise article ("The most common mistake I see is people moving too quickly or bouncing through the motion") teaches the bodyweight raise, another version of the movement, so it is not counted here (R-LB7-5); counted, it would name bouncing (Motra list item 1), which shows only as speed, so the drawn fault (locked knees) would not change, though handlingMistakes[0] would move to bouncing. Step 2: one named fault is tied to harm: locking the knees (Motra's list item 2, "Locking knees", c6), by two sources: Motra's "Maintain slight knee bend to protect joints" (D-SUP-PROTECT: the cue that corrects the fault protects a named body part) and Fitness Volt's "Keep your knees slightly bent but stable throughout the exercise to avoid strain." ('strain' counts as harm by the lb6 precedent) (c5). Set aside at step 2: "Avoid excessive weight to prevent Achilles strain" (c15) ties harm to the load, which is not a candidate; Fitness Volt's "heavy calf raises put a lot of vertical stress on your spine, which can cause compression of the intervertebral disks" and "could even cause back pain" (c17) are about the load on the shoulders and name no fault; its "Even padded standing calf raise machines put a lot of pressure on your shoulders." is about the machine, and 'pressure' is not an LR-31 harm word; Motra's "Stop if sharp pain occurs" (c16) names no fault, and its "When to Avoid" items ("Achilles tendonitis", "Lower back issues", "Recent ankle injury") are conditions; Fitness Volt's "this exercise stresses all three calf muscles relatively equally" is about muscles, "While standing calf raises are a safe and effective exercise" names no fault, and "seated calf raises are very back-friendly and suitable for exercisers with lower back pain" and "seated calf raises can hurt your legs" are another exercise; BarBend's uncited "help protect your Achilles tendon against possible injury" and "help prevent calf strains" are benefits of calf training, not a fault; Fitness Volt's "Do not overstretch your calves during the negative portion of the exercise." (c10) states no harm; Motra's other list items, "Bouncing at bottom", "Leaning forward" and "Partial range of motion" (c6), are tied to no harm (Fitness Volt's "half reps get half results!" is in its seated tips and states no harm). Step 3 is not needed; it would give bouncing at the bottom, first on Motra's list, which is seen only as speed. drawable true: the side view shows a straight, locked knee against a slightly bent one, a still sign. handlingMistakes keeps Motra's list order after the top fault: bouncing at the bottom (speed only), then leaning forward.

tells.text: Heels rise as high as you can

tempo.text: Down 2 and up 2 are Motra's 2-1-2 (c19, WEAK), read in its Tempo tooltip's order: lowering, bottom pause, lifting, top pause (R-LB6-2, R-LB6-7); the page shows three numbers, read as the first three, with no top-pause seconds. Its 1 s bottom pause sits at the stretch with the heels low, so it is named here and not written in pause (LR-33). Pause 1 is the pause right after the lift: Motra's "Squeeze calves at the top and hold briefly." and Fitness Volt's "At the top, pause briefly to squeeze your calf muscles." give no seconds, so the 1 s is a drawing convention (c20, WEAK; LR-33).

libraryDiff.why: calves primary matches every read source (c13; Kinoshita's growth data, c14). Motra alone lists glutes as secondary and hamstrings and abs as accessory; no other read source does, so they are not added.

Anchor: Motra's machine standing calf raise page, read in full (How to Perform, Coaching Tips, Tempo with its tooltip, Range of Motion, Safety, Common Mistakes). Fitness Volt's seated-vs-standing article (both how-to sections, pro tips, pros and cons), Fitness Volt's machine standing calf raise guide and StrengthLog's standing calf raise page were read in full, and the Kinoshita 2023 abstract through efetch.
Shared cards: get-in-out (shared/get-in-out.json) leaves standing_calf_raise out of appliesTo (its appliesToWhy: standing); selector-pin does not list it. Nothing is taken from either.
Related card cards/leg_press_calf_raise.json was read for shape only; no line or claim is carried from it. Every line here rests on this card's own fetched claims.

Stretch depth conflict (c10): Motra says a full stretch below the platform, Fitness Volt's article as much as comfortably possible, and Fitness Volt's machine guide warns not to overstretch. The card draws and says a full but comfortable stretch.

The Achilles feel row keeps Motra's stop quote (c16, "Stop if sharp pain occurs"; R-LB3-4, R-LB6-6). No shared red-flag box covers the ankle, so its redFlag is null. The knee row is place + the source's fault + fix (LR-6), linking the knee box.
The spine risk (c17) keeps Fitness Volt's 'could even'. No back feel row is written: no source gives a fix for it beyond going cautiously with existing back issues, so no back box is linked (LR-6).

Read and not cited: ACE's Calf Raises page (exercise-library/51) is the barbell-on-the-back version on the floor, another version, so it is not used; ACE's Calf Raise page (exercise-library/294) is a seated, straight-leg selectorized machine, another exercise. BarBend has no standing calf raise page (barbend.com/standing-calf-raise/ 404); its best-calf-exercises list has no standing machine section.
